title: Review: Strong and weak acids; Neutralisation and salts; Oxidation states and naming
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for OCR A-level (A) Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: RX02#t3 term and clue written for the game; RX02#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB03#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB03#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB03#N.11, AB04#N.4, RX02#N.10, AB03#N.4a, AB04#N.15, RX02#N.4a, AB03#N.7, AB04#N.10, RX02#N.8, AB03#N.3a, RX02#N.9. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Metal hydride
items.clue: Compound such as NaH or CaH₂ in which H is −1.

items.label: Peroxide
items.clue: Compound such as H₂O₂ or Na₂O₂ in which O is −1.

items.label: Concentration
items.clue: The amount of a dissolved substance per unit volume.

items.label: Strong acid
items.clue: Dissociates effectively completely in water, as HNO₃ does.

questions.stem: Which statement about solutions P and Q is correct? P is 5.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ HCl(aq). Q is 0.50 mol dm⁻³ CH₃COOH(aq), measured pH 2.53.

options.text: P has the lower pH, as a strong acid always has a lower pH than a weak one.
P has the higher pH, even though HCl is the stronger acid.
CH₃COOH must be a strong acid, as Q has a lower pH than P.
HCl is a weak acid in P, as its concentration is low.

questions.explanation: P: pH = −log₁₀(5.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 3.30. Only about 1 in 170 CH₃COOH molecules in Q dissociates, but Q is 1000 times more concentrated, so [H⁺] ≈ 2.95 × 10⁻³, pH 2.53. pH depends on concentration as well as strength.

questions.stem: Which reaction produces a salt and water, with no other product?

options.text: Potassium carbonate with hydrochloric acid
Ammonia with sulfuric acid
Barium hydroxide with nitric acid
Zinc with hydrochloric acid

questions.explanation: Each OH⁻ takes one H⁺ to form water: Ba(OH)₂ + 2HNO₃ → Ba(NO₃)₂ + 2H₂O.

questions.stem: Chlorine is −1 in the chloride ion, Cl⁻, but +1 in the hypochlorite ion, ClO⁻ (in bleach). Which explains the +1?

options.text: The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ has lost a proton to the oxygen atom, leaving chlorine with a +1 charge.
Oxygen always has the oxidation number −1 in an ion with one negative charge.
Oxygen is more electronegative than chlorine, so it is assigned the shared electrons in the Cl–O bond.
The chlorine atom in ClO⁻ carries a real charge of +1, as in a Cl⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: O takes both shared electrons and is −2; the total must be −1, so x + (−2) = −1 and Cl is +1. In Cl⁻, chlorine holds an extra electron: −1.

questions.stem: Solution X is 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ KOH(aq). Solution Y is 2.0 mol dm⁻³ NH₃(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: NH₃ is the stronger base, as solution Y is more concentrated.
NH₃ is not a base, as its formula contains no OH group.
KOH is the stronger base, as it is fully dissociated.
Both are strong bases, as both release OH⁻ ions in water.

questions.explanation: Strength is the extent of dissociation, not concentration. KOH is fully dissociated even when dilute; NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻ lies well to the left.

questions.stem: Baking powder contains sodium hydrogencarbonate and a solid acid. When the cake batter gets wet, the two react. Why does the cake rise?

options.text: HCO₃⁻ accepts H⁺ from the acid, giving water and carbon dioxide gas.
The acid reacts with sodium, giving hydrogen gas.
A salt and water form, as in every neutralisation, and the steam lifts the cake.
HCO₃⁻ donates H⁺ to the acid, giving CO₃²⁻ and a gas.

questions.explanation: HCO₃⁻ + H⁺ → H₂O + CO₂. The bubbles of CO₂ make the batter rise, just as CO₂ from a carbonate antacid makes you burp.

questions.stem: What are the oxidation numbers of hydrogen in sodium hydride, NaH, and of oxygen in sodium peroxide, Na₂O₂?
questions.explanation: In NaH, Na is +1, so H is −1 (the hydride ion). In Na₂O₂, 2(+1) + 2x = 0, so O is −1 (the peroxide ion, O₂²⁻).

questions.stem: Methanoic acid is a weak acid: HCOOH(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ HCOO⁻(aq) + H₃O⁺(aq). Which statement is correct?

options.text: The equilibrium lies to the right, as all acids dissociate in water.
The equilibrium lies to the left, as HCOO⁻ is a weaker base than H₂O.
The equilibrium lies to the right, as HCOO⁻ is the weaker of the two bases.
The equilibrium lies to the left, as H₃O⁺ is a stronger acid than HCOOH.

questions.explanation: Equilibrium favours the weaker acid and weaker base. HCOOH is weaker than H₃O⁺, and H₂O weaker than HCOO⁻, so the left is favoured: few molecules dissociate.

questions.stem: What are the parent acid and parent base of ammonium methanoate, HCOONH₄?

options.text: Parent acid HCOO⁻; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₄⁺
Parent acid NH₃; parent base HCOOH
Parent acid HCOOH; parent base NH₃

questions.explanation: The anion HCOO⁻ comes from methanoic acid; the cation NH₄⁺ formed when NH₃ accepted a proton. HCOOH + NH₃ → HCOONH₄.

options.text: K₂Cr₂O₇, potassium dichromate(VI)
K₂MnO₄, potassium manganate(IV)
Fe₂(SO₄)₃, iron(VI) sulfate
MnCl₂, manganese(VII) chloride

questions.explanation: 2(+1) + 2x + 7(−2) = 0 gives 2x = +12, so each Cr is +6. The numeral is per atom.

questions.stem: A solution of nitric acid, HNO₃(aq), has a concentration of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Which statement about this solution is correct?

options.text: It is a weak acid, as its concentration is low.
It contains mainly HNO₃ molecules with a few ions.
It is a dilute solution of an acid that is fully dissociated.
It is neutral, as this much water neutralises the acid.

questions.explanation: HNO₃ → H⁺ + NO₃⁻ completely, so [H⁺] = 0.0010 mol dm⁻³. Strength and concentration are independent.

questions.stem: What is the formula of sodium chlorate(III)?

options.text: NaClO₃
Na₃ClO
NaCl₃O
NaClO₂

questions.explanation: In ClO₂⁻, x + 2(−2) = −1, so Cl = +3. One Na⁺ balances the 1− charge.
